1.title: VT (Late Harvest) vs SGN (Noble-Rot Selection): A Fundamental Difference in Flavour Logic
1.items.0.label: Vendanges Tardives (Late Harvest)
1.items.0.desc: The grapes are picked several weeks after the normal harvest, reaching a state of "overripeness" (surmaturité) — drying and concentration is the main effect. The variety's own identity and aroma character remain clearly recognisable, simply layered with greater concentration and power.
1.items.1.label: Sélection de Grains Nobles (Noble-Rot Selection)
1.items.1.desc: Through several passes of picking (tries successives), only berries infected with noble rot (Botrytis cinerea) are selected — noble-rot flavour dominates and varietal identity is relatively veiled. It shows rich honey aromas, an extremely powerful structure, a round, viscous texture and a long finish.
2.title: Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris: The Two Mainstays of Noble Rot
2.html:
Gewurztraminer: even in ordinary vintages it often carries a touch of residual sugar, and the VT version is more exuberant and heady — roses, lychee and spice stacking layer upon layer; the SGN version is almost liquid flower nectar, suited to blue cheese or as a prized bottle for sipping on its own after a meal.

Pinot Gris: itself the fullest-bodied of the Alsace white varieties, its VT version is richer and rounder still, with honey and roasted nut notes; the VT of good vintages is often paired with luxurious dishes such as foie gras and truffle, while the SGN version develops deep layers of candied fruit and caramel.
3.title: Riesling and Muscat: Two with the Strictest Thresholds but Very Different Styles
3.html:
Although Riesling's VT / SGN sugar thresholds are lower than those of Gewurztraminer / Pinot Gris, its naturally high acidity lets it keep a striking freshness even at high sugar levels — the sweet-acid balance is the most charming aspect of Riesling noble-rot sweet wines, and their ageing potential is especially outstanding.

The VT / SGN versions of Muscat are relatively rare (the variety with the smallest production) but especially precious — its exuberant grape aromas become even more heady and charming under the concentrating effect of noble-rot sweet wine, making it the most exotic noble-rot sweet wine style of the four varieties.
4.question: What is the most fundamental difference in flavour logic between VT (Late Harvest) and SGN (Noble-Rot Selection)?
4.options.0: VT can use only white grapes and SGN only black grapes
4.options.1: VT keeps varietal identity with an added concentration effect; SGN is dominated by noble-rot flavour, with varietal identity relatively veiled
4.options.2: VT is always sweeter than SGN
4.options.3: The two are made in exactly the same way, just with different names
4.explanation: For VT (Late Harvest), the grapes merely reach a state of "overripeness", the variety's own aroma character remains clearly recognisable, simply layered with a concentration effect; for SGN (Noble-Rot Selection), several passes of picking select only berries infected with noble rot, and the flavour is dominated by Botrytis cinerea, with varietal identity relatively veiled, replaced by rich, complex aromas of honey and candied fruit.
5.message: Noble-rot sweet wine styles of the four noble varieties complete!
5.keyPoints.0: VT: added concentration effect, clear varietal identity; SGN: noble-rot flavour dominates, rich and complex, with honey and candied fruit notes
5.keyPoints.1: Gewurztraminer: the noble-rot version is the most exuberant and gorgeous, with SGN almost liquid flower nectar
5.keyPoints.2: Pinot Gris: the fullest and richest, with VT often paired with luxurious dishes such as foie gras and truffle
5.keyPoints.3: Riesling: its high-acid variety character keeps noble-rot sweet wines fresh and balanced, with the best ageing potential
5.keyPoints.4: Muscat: the smallest production and the rarest, the noble-rot version the most exotic
